title: The Transitus (3 October 1226)
hookLine: Francis dies lying on the bare ground singing Psalm 141

lines: EVENING, AT SAINT MARY OF THE ANGELS.
LAY ME ON THE BARE GROUND.
cards: Evening, at the little church of Saint Mary of the Angels below Assisi. Francis is dying, and he knows it. His brothers crowd around.
He's blind or nearly, worn out, and the early lives say he carries wounds in his hands and side. He asks for something strange: take off my habit, and lay me on the bare ground. No bed, no pillow.
Just the earth he called sister and mother. Then, the old biographers say, he began to sing. Today, the night Francis died, and the name his brothers gave it.

teach.b: Franciscans call that night the Transitus, Latin for a passing over. Not an ending, a crossing.

The word echoes the Gospel Francis asked to hear that evening, John chapter thirteen, which opens in the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus knowing that his hour was come, that he should pass out of this world to the Father."
Francis wanted to die the way his Lord had passed: poor, stripped, among friends. The early lives tell it in pieces. He blesses the brothers around him.
In Saint Bonaventure's telling, he says he has done his part; may Christ teach them theirs.

teach.h: PSALM 141, SUNG ON THE BARE GROUND.
teach.b: Then he sings Psalm one hundred forty-one, as numbered in the Latin Bible the friars prayed: "I cried to the Lord with my voice." Near the end it asks: "Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name."

A dying man asking to be let out, and calling it praise. Earlier, Francis had added a last verse to his Canticle of the Creatures, praising God for our Sister Bodily Death, whom no one living can escape.
Celano tells that when death came near, Francis greeted it as family: welcome, my sister death. The man who called the sun brother called death sister too.

teach.h: BRING MY SOUL OUT OF PRISON.
teach.b: Bonaventure adds a quiet detail: larks, birds of daylight, gathered over the roof at dusk and sang. Sign or lovely story, the brothers remembered it.
And if death feels close or wanted for you tonight, please don't carry that alone: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

how: Franciscans and some parishes keep a Transitus service on the eve of Saint Francis's feast, retelling his death with readings, Psalm 141 and his Canticle of the Creatures, often by candlelight.

o: the friars' long walk carrying Francis's body to Rome
Francis's death, remembered as a passing over
a Latin hymn sung at the end of every Mass

p: I cried to the Lord with my voice
greeted by Francis as a sister

s: Francis died in a fine bed, surrounded by honors
he asked his brothers to lay him on the bare ground, stripped of his habit.
Francis greeted his death as a sister
Celano tells it: welcome, my sister death. he had already praised God for Sister Bodily Death in his Canticle.
Transitus is just Latin for funeral
it means a passing over, an echo of John 13, where Jesus passes out of this world to the Father.

games.q: you're Francis, and you know tonight is your last. your brothers ask what you want. what do you ask for?
o: a soft bed and a quiet room.
to be laid on the bare ground, and to hear the Gospel.
to be carried to a great cathedral.
games.why: he asked to lie on the bare earth, heard John 13 read, and sang Psalm 141. poor at the end, as at the start.

practice: Lie flat if you can, on the floor or a bed, arms loose, or lean back and let your body be heavy, and feel the ground holding you up.

If you pray, say the line Francis sang, I cried to the Lord with my voice, and rest, then the other: bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name; if not, just notice how it feels to be held, with nothing to do.

wordCard.voice: The Transitus. Francis's passing over: dying on the bare ground, singing a psalm, greeting death as his sister. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a passing over, a crossing; the Franciscan name for the night of Francis's death.

carryVoice: Your line: welcome, sister death. For Francis, even the last night was a crossing, met among friends. Go gently tonight.
